Daurian pika, Ochotona dauurica, is a small lagomorph inhabiting the steppes and alpine meadows of central and eastern Asia. During the active metabolic phase, individuals maintain a core body temperature of approximately 40.1 °C [T = 40.1 °C], which is notably high for a mammal of its size. Under these thermal conditions, resting metabolic rate measurements, obtained via closed-circuit respirometry, indicate a basal oxygen consumption of 249 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 249 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at a temperature of 40.1 °C [T = 40.1 °C]. This elevated metabolic demand is likely a consequence of the species' endothermic lifestyle in a cold, seasonal environment. Field-based studies have documented that a single female can produce up to three litters annually, with each litter containing between one and eleven pups [N_R_i = each litter containing between one and eleven pups], though the mean litter size is approximately 4.8 offspring. Across multiple breeding seasons, the combination of moderate litter sizes and frequent reproductive events, at approximately 3 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 3 litters per year], allows Daurian pika populations to persist in unpredictable, resource-limited habitats.

Neonatal development in Daurian pika begins in utero with a gestation period lasting approximately 30 days [tg = approximately 30 days] when measured at the typical maternal body temperature of 40.1 °C [T = 40.1 °C]. Although reported gestation times for other Ochotona species range from 21 to 24 days, the slightly longer duration observed in O. dauurica may reflect adaptations to the cooler thermal regime of its steppe environment. At the moment of parturition, newborn individuals are altricial, with an average birth mass of roughly 9 grams [Wwb = roughly 9 grams], a value derived from comparative data on the American pika (Ochotona princeps). This modest neonatal mass is consistent with the energetic constraints imposed by the high basal metabolic rate of the mother. The pre-weaning stage is relatively short-lived; the time since birth at weaning is approximately 21 days since birth [tx = approximately 21 days since birth] under standard thermal conditions of 40.1 °C [T = 40.1 °C]. At this point, the average wet weight at weaning is around 90 grams [Wwx = around 90 grams], representing a tenfold increase in body mass from birth, an exceptionally rapid growth phase for a small-bodied mammal.

Following the weaning phase, juvenile Daurian pikas undergo a rapid period of somatic growth to achieve their ultimate adult body mass. Maximum adult wet weight in this species is 249 grams [Wwi = 249 grams], a value that is attained within the first several months of life. This substantial increase in mass aligns with the species' need to build adequate lipid and protein stores before the onset of winter. Reproductive maturity is reached relatively early in life; the time since birth at puberty is recorded as approximately 21 days since birth [tp = approximately 21 days since birth] when the ambient temperature is maintained at 40.1 °C [T = 40.1 °C]. This remarkably accelerated sexual maturation is among the fastest documented in lagomorphs and is likely an adaptation to the short, favorable growing season characteristic of high-latitude steppe habitats. Consequently, females from early-season litters are often capable of contributing to the breeding population within the same calendar year, thereby maximizing annual recruitment and facilitating population persistence in strongly seasonal environments.

Longevity in Daurian pika is notably compressed relative to other mammals of comparable body size, with the maximum lifespan recorded at 2.3 years [am = 2.3 years] for individuals living under natural conditions at a body temperature of 40.1 °C [T = 40.1 °C]. This short lifespan, equivalent to approximately 840 days when expressed as a total duration, imposes strong selective pressure for early and repeated reproduction. The physiological costs of maintaining a high basal metabolic rate, coupled with the energetic demands of frequent breeding and rapid growth, likely contribute to accelerated senescence and a brief reproductive window. Comparative analyses with other ochotonids confirm that Daurian pika occupies the short-lived, high-fecundity end of the lagomorph life-history continuum, a pattern that is consistent with its role as a staple prey species for a variety of avian and mammalian predators across the Central Asian steppe ecosystem.

From an ecological perspective, the life-history strategy of Daurian pika is tightly coupled to the seasonal availability of herbaceous forage. During the peak growing season, when ambient temperatures are high enough to support a body temperature of 40.1 °C [T = 40.1 °C], females are capable of producing up to three litters per year [F_R_i = up to three litters per year], each with an average of 4.8 pups per litter [N_R_i = 4.8 pups per litter]. This reproductive output is essential for maintaining population density in the face of high predation pressure. The species' birth mass of roughly 9 grams [Wwb = roughly 9 grams] may also serve to minimize the initial energy investment per offspring, allowing females to allocate more resources toward the rapid production of subsequent litters. Within a single year, a dominant female can produce over 24 pups, underscoring the species' remarkable capacity for population irruption following favorable climatic conditions. Such demographic flexibility is a hallmark of small-bodied, short-lived mammalian herbivores occupying unpredictable, high-latitude environments.
